message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
The pilot data look solid, and most of the arithmetic is correct. But the study's central claim about flats contradicts its own table, the tonnage projection uses a participation rate that doesn't appear in the pilot results, and the disposal saving assumes treatment capacity that Brookfield has said it can't provide. Once these are corrected, the service is no longer fully covered by the provisional funding.

## What checks out

- **Table 1 is internally consistent.** 66%, 21% and 57% all match their household counts.
- **The cost table adds up.** £990,000 of vehicles over 7 years is £141,400 a year. Crews of 12 × £34,000 come to £408,000. The total is £733,400.
- **The diversion saving per tonne is right.** £112 − £38 = £74, and the arithmetic in the projection is consistent with its stated inputs.
- **The contamination and satisfaction results are good news** and worth reporting.

## 1. Participation was not "broadly similar" in houses and flats

Table 1 shows **66% participation in houses and 21% in flats**, so houses participated more than three times as much. Flats also produced less food waste per participating household, 1.4 kg against 1.9 kg.

Section 2's statement that participation was "broadly similar," and the conclusion that no separate approach for flats is needed, run directly against the data. Low participation in flats is a well-known pattern, usually because individual outdoor caddies don't suit communal bin stores. The pilot is evidence that flats *do* need a different approach, such as communal food bins, bin-store signage and liaison with managing agents.

## 2. The projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't produce

Section 3 applies **"the pilot's 64% participation rate."** But the pilot's overall rate was **57%**, and neither housing type was 64%. It also applies 1.9 kg a week to every participating household, including flats, which averaged 1.4 kg.

The district has about 20% flats, which is the same as the pilot (800 of 4,000). So the pilot results can be applied by housing type directly:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ≈ 2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ≈ 159 |
| **Total** | **52,000** | | | **≈ 2,870** |

That's about **420 tonnes (13%) less** than the 3,290 in the study. The diversion saving falls from £243,000 to about **£212,500**.

## 3. Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage

Section 4 says Brookfield can offer **up to 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. That's well below either projection, whether 3,290 or about 2,870 tonnes. The remaining 1,070 tonnes or so would have to go to the plant **46 miles away**, at a gate fee the study doesn't give and with haulage costs that aren't in Table 2.

Applying the £74-a-tonne saving to the full tonnage is therefore unsupported. The only saving that's evidenced is on the 1,800 tonnes at Brookfield, about **£133,000**. The saving on the rest could be small or even negative once haulage is included. Your summary's description of treatment as "local" is only partly true.

## 4. The funding conclusion doesn't hold

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | Against £520k provisional allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| As in the study | £243,000 | £490,400 | £29,600 surplus |
| Corrected tonnage, all at Brookfield rates | ~£212,500 | ~£520,900 | roughly break-even |
| Saving only on 1,800 t at Brookfield | ~£133,200 | ~£600,200 | **~£80,000 shortfall**, before haulage |

The third row is the only one consistent with Brookfield's confirmed capacity. Even the study's own figure left a margin of only about 6% against an allocation that is still **provisional**. "Fully funded" should not appear in the recommendation as it stands.

## 5. Costs that appear to be missing

Your summary says every cost line is shown, but several items mentioned or implied in the study aren't costed:

- **Haulage to the second AD plant** for tonnage above 1,800 tonnes, as above.
- **The dedicated phone line and web page** in section 6.
- **Recruitment and training** for 12 new operatives.
- **Relief cover:** six crews of two with no allowance for sickness or holiday, and no spare vehicle for breakdowns or maintenance.
- **The flats approach**, such as communal bins and engagement, if the Council adopts one in response to point 1.

Some of these may be included in other lines. If so, the study should say which.

## 6. Smaller points

- **The timetable has no slack.** Vehicles arrive in March, crews train in March, and caddies go to 52,000 households in March, with collections starting on 5 April. A delay in vehicle delivery pushes back the start date directly. It's worth stating a contingency, such as hired vehicles.
- **The basis of the survey isn't given.** "81% of surveyed pilot households" doesn't say how many were surveyed or whether non-participants responded. People who use a service are more likely to answer a survey about it.
- **The statutory deadline:** my understanding is that under Simpler Recycling, most English councils were expected to start weekly food waste collections from 31 March 2026, with transitional arrangements for some. If Thornbury's April 2027 start depends on such an arrangement, the study should say so. Please check this against current DEFRA guidance.

## Suggested changes before Cabinet

1. Correct section 2 to report the difference between houses and flats honestly, and add a costed approach for flats.
2. Re-base the projection on the participation rates and yields for each housing type, giving about 2,870 tonnes.
3. Address Brookfield's 1,800-tonne cap by giving the second plant's gate fee and haulage cost, or by securing extra capacity, and recalculate the saving.
4. Complete the cost table, including relief cover, a spare vehicle, the contact line and recruitment.
5. Replace "fully funded" with a funding position that shows sensitivity to the final new-burdens allocation.

The pilot is useful evidence and the case for the service may well stand. As written, though, the study rests on three points the data contradict: that flats behave like houses, that participation is 64%, and that Brookfield can take all the waste.
